name: Salt glow

card.summary: A hydrotherapy-style salt rub, associated with the Battle Creek Sanitarium, used to leave the skin looking fresh and glowing.
card.note: Abrasive on sensitive or broken skin.

quick.overview:
A salt glow is a full-body rub in which wet salt is massaged over the skin, then rinsed, to leave it pink and smooth. It was a named treatment in the baths-and-rubs regimens of John Harvey Kellogg's Battle Creek Sanitarium.

Its appearance payoff is exfoliation and a flushed, fresh look. Sanitarium baths were promoted for health and skin conditions [1]; no studies have tested the salt glow.
quick.how: It is done as a spa-style body scrub, coarse salt rubbed over damp skin and rinsed. Modern versions are sold as salt scrubs.
quick.risks: Rubbing salt on skin can sting and irritate, particularly on cuts, sunburn or conditions such as eczema.

lead: The salt glow is a body treatment in which salt is rubbed over the skin to exfoliate and stimulate it. It is associated with the Battle Creek Sanitarium in Michigan, run by John Harvey Kellogg, which advertised 46 kinds of baths in 1907 [1].

The expected effect on looks is smoother, pinker, fresh-looking skin after the rub. Kellogg recommended the sanitarium's baths for conditions including skin diseases [1]. No clinical studies exist on the salt glow.

angle.text: The rub physically exfoliates and flushes the skin, leaving it smoother and rosier for a while after.

paras: The Battle Creek Sanitarium offered many hydrotherapy procedures; a 1907 advertisement boasted 46 kinds of baths, and Kellogg recommended them for skin diseases and other complaints [1].
